item.title: What Books Did to My Brain (2021)
item.description: Reads I finished or found enriching to my life
item.content:encoded:
This is a weird time to talk about years. I don’t know about you, but my brain stopped recording time in December 2020. To me, we’re still in 2020 — we’re just now in Omicron season.

The fact that time now is a permeable, amorphous, indiscrete phenomenon makes writing a “yearly” book list feel like a strange endeavor — almost a dishonest one. And yet, I look back on the last 12 months with a distinct gratitude. I came out of a political campaign, started a new job in the nonprofit sector, and embraced the emptiness that can come along with setting a new life direction. It’s a time when I learned and grew without knowing exactly where it would take me. And I am proud of that.

Last year, books helped me slow down and reflect. As Ezra Klein remarks from Nicholas Carr’s The Shallows, the main value of a book comes often not from its ideas but from the time you spend engaging with them. Reading, an admittedly a difficult activity for me as a citizen of the digital age, is a rare opportunity to slow down and focus — to reflect and find a calming peace in both text and in the inner worlds of ourselves.

Here’s a list of books that were part of my journey.

  • A Promised Land, Vol. 1, by Barack Obama

  • The Shallows: What the Internet is Doing to Our Brains, by Nicholas Carr

  • The Overstory, by Richard Powers

  • Bewilderment, by Richard Powers

  • Change: How to Make Big Things Happen, by Damon Centola

  • Don’t Think of An Elephant, by George Lakoff

  • Four Thousand Weeks: Time Management for Mortals, by Oliver Burkeman

  • Superforecasters, by Philip E. Tetlock and Dan Gardner

  • Everything is Obvious (Once You Know the Answer), by Duncan Watts

  • State of Resistance, by Manuel Pastor

  • Think Again, by Adam Grant

  • Lead From the Outside, by Stacey Abrams

  • Atomic Habits, by James Clear

  • The Stranger, by Albert Camus

And here’s some books I didn’t finish but appreciated:

  • How to Break Up With Your Phone, by Catherine Price

  • Stories of Your Life (And Others), by Ted Chiang

  • The Anthropocene: Reviewed, by John Green

  • Why Nations Fail, by Daron Acemoglu and James A. Robinson

  • Originals, by Adam Grant

  • Why Civil Resistance Works, by Erica Chenoweth

  • The Divide, by Jason Hickel

  • Hobos, Hustlers, and Backsliders, by Teresa Gowan

  • The Coddling of the American Mind, by Greg Lukianoff & Jonathan Haidt

  • Animal, Vegetable, Junk, by Mark Bittman

  • America’s Boy, by James Hamilton-Paterson

  • The LSAT Trainer, by Mike Kim (joking, kind of)

Here are some reflections on the books that left the biggest impressions on me.

Non-Fiction

A Promised Land, Vol. 1, by Barack Obama. Long a believer in change yet remarking at its difficulty, I picked up Obama’s latest biography after losing an election I put my heart and soul into. Politics is a tough game. And I found that the reflections of a former president — both on the challenges of winning an election to the constraints that can come from occupying even of the most powerful positions in the world — offered clarity for me as I decompressed from intensely a local grassroots campaign.

Two books I enjoyed covered similar themes. Lead from the Outside, an inspiring biography by Georgia gubernatorial candidate Stacey Abrams, gave me an appreciation for the unique challenges often faced by people of color in entering public service. And State of Resistance, an activist handbook-esque history by Manuel Pastor, reminds us that while America today may seem to be spiraling into individualism and inequality, California was not always a liberal standard bearer — and that it flipped decades ago from being a Reagan-led conservative stronghold to its current eminence as a national progressive leader.

A few books I read to tune up and tinker with my sputtering engine of a brain. Think Again by Adam Grant is a call for us to reflect on our assumptions, change worldviews with humility, and engage with others constructively. Typifying the contrasting modes of thought of preachers (those who pronounce their views), prosecutors (those who tear down the views of others), and politicians (those who change views to gain the support of others), he encourages us to adopt another mental state — that of scientists (whose seek truth). Having finished a political campaign where all P’s came into play, I appreciated reflecting on my own cognitive blind spots with a few hundred pages of cognitive tips and pithy anecdotes.

Also offering cognitive boons, Superforecasters by Philip E. Tetlock and Dan Gardner totally changed how I organize my thoughts. Based on the Good Judgement Project, possibly the most rigorous and methodical study of how to more accurately forecast the future, the books made me feel like I finally understood the political egg heads around me who always seemed to get things right. Technically about prediction, I think its lessons are also applicable to forming accurate opinions about the world (for example, whether industrialization has done more harm than good).

One of my favorite insights is the usefulness of taking the “outside” view on predictions. For example, if you and I were to predict whether the recent marriage of our friend would end in divorce, we shouldn’t start with weighing all of the inside characteristics of their relationship — whether they share interests, how often they fight, etc. Instead, we would first look to general marriage statistics — say, the U.S. divorce rate of 41% — to get an outside view of marriages in general. Then we would look at the specifics of their marriage to “update” our prediction up or down from this baseline probability. With each fight or bond-solidifying experience, we can increase or decrease our probability assessment based on the experience and how many came before it. The authors explain it way better than I do, and their ideas helped my brain hurt less when juggling lots of information. (It gets easier over time — and you might find it so fun you start a Google Sheet prediction ring with your friends).

Change: How to Make Big Things Happen, by Damon Centola, was perhaps the most foundational social science book on my understanding of social change. First, because it provided scientific grounding for many of my intuitions on how to change social norms. Second, because some of the predictions I made after reading the book — were upended multiple times in 2021. As Tetlock and Gardner suggest, I may have been well-served to start from a more general outside view of political campaigns and social movements, then applied these more narrow insights on how social networks influence social change, updating my beliefs incrementally rather than throwing out my faith all at once. In any case, Centola’s Change is a thought-provoking framework on how the dramatic events we see on our Instagram stories facilitate transformative changes around you and me.

Also in this category is Everything is Obvious (Once You Know the Answer), by Duncan Watts. My friend Wayne Hsiung has been constantly talking about this book (and did a fascinating podcast with the author). When I finally picked it up, I found it a powerful reminder of how “common sense” can provide enticingly obvious yet false explanations for past events and lull us into misleading confidence in predicting the world to come. With memorably convincing anecdotes (of course farmers were better soldiers in WWII!), I was left with an urgent sense that I need to seek real evidence — not simply rely on gut feelings — to before I resolutely decide what is true about the world. If you want to be intellectually humbled, read this book.

Don’t Think of An Elephant by George Lakoff is one I’ve put off and am glad I finally got through. It was a tough read for me because it’s foundational in roaring debates among activists on movement strategy, framing, and messaging. I finally finished it only by committing not to overanalyze it page-by-page but simply take in its overall lessons and allow them to suffuse over time into my lived everyday experience. The lessons to many may be counterintuitive, and I’ve spent much time figuring out what its lessons really mean for what we should do as activists. Also in this category is Erica Chenoweths’ social movement case study collection of Why Civil Resistance Works. Both are worthy reads for social justice activists.

Why Nations Fail, by Daron Acemoglu and James Robinson. Enough people — a list including effective altruists, intermediate economics professors, and city council candidates — have recommended this book to me that I felt compelled to eventually check it out. I did, partially, and appreciated the read. Message me to discuss.

Finally, The Shallows by Nicholas Carr is worth its own blog post. In his review, Ezra Klein remarked that the value of a book comes not from the ideas of the text, but rather the time you spend engaging with it. I’ve found this to be true, and it changed how and how often I read. The book fascinatingly illustrates the neuroscience behind focus and reading. And it argues, persuasively and urgently, that these skills and modes of being are being disastrously undermined by the internet and social media.

Subscribe now

Our evolution has primed our brains to scatter our focus — to dart our attention towards a rustle in the leaves, or a pair of eyes in the dark. When they emerged in history, books and written text for the first time allowed us to hone our attention more deeply — to develop a silent inner voice that enabled reading complex meandering thoughts and the ability to derive meaning from it.

The internet undermines that. It takes us away from centuries of training our brains back to a time when our attention was scattered by constant threat — though this time, the danger is less real in terms of violence and more digital and psychologically insidious. The internet reverts our brain to a state of scattered attention that focuses not on ever-possible threat, but a deafening lack of meaning. Stay tuned for a post here.

Stories (fiction)

Richard Powers’ Pulitzer Prize-winning magnum opus The Overstory and his shorter Bewilderment tore me apart and put me back together several times over.

The empathy that The Overstory famously engenders for trees is the same that Bewilderment does for (non-human) animals. I so often felt giddy at the short story’s relatability. One love interest is an animal rights lawyer, and one meal is arguably the quintessential meal of veganism: “For lunch, I scrambled tofu, using the exact ratio of black salt and nutritional yeast that [my son] loved.”

Ezra Klein captured my feelings on Bewilderment: “It is a devastating book. We live in a maddening world where simply saying what we should do constrains the limits of what we will do.”

Peppering the story — one of a single father and his neurodivergent son — with references to broader political and cultural trends, Powers makes the larger world we are living through feel so personal and urgent. Ezra reviews,

It is about our cognition, our brainwaves, the way we can live in a time of wonders, but a time also of horrors — of climate crisis and mass extinction and poverty that doesn’t need to be there and violence — how we can live in that time and see nothing but normalcy, sometimes see nothing but ourselves. It’s about the limits of our cognitive empathy and what it would take to change them and what we do to those among us who aren’t so limited. It is an enchanting and — my God — it is a devastating book.

And,

Whether your concern is climate or it’s poverty or it’s animal suffering or it’s global health or any of a list we could keep doing, there is just a chasm between what we should do and what we will.

And what makes that even worse is that often, insisting on what we should do… can lead to tremendous political backlash. It can lead to a shrinking of what we will do.

The books capture what many — especially young people — may experience now as polarization and climate anxiety. The empathy that Powers fosters for nature and animals enables the in-story political dynamics to tear us emotionally apart. They instilled in me a deeper sense of connection and tragedy to our collective anthropocene’s mark on the world. The books are devastatingly relatable, but in a weird way, peacefully relatable and empowering.

These stories, too, enhanced my life and helped chip away at my embarrassing years-long neglect of fiction. Stories of Your Life (And Others), by Ted Chiang (who wrote the story that inspired the awesome movie Arrival), and The Anthropocene: Reviewed, by my childhood hero John Green, reminded me the joy of immersing myself in an imagined world and the insights this can glean on our own.

Philosophy & Self Help

(Two categories that I insist are, at their best, basically the same)

Finally, there are some philosophy and self-help books I enjoyed — ones that I felt I needed to read as a twenty-something-year-old in the tumultuous year of twenty-twenty-too. Atomic Habits, by James Clear, and How to Break Up With Your Phone, by Catherine Price, were mere text on pages that have so far improved my life for the better. Thank you.

Four Thousand Weeks: Time Management for Mortals by Oliver Burkeman met me at the perfect time. I listened to this driving back from my parents’ house during the 2021/2022 Omicron Winter Games. Gently carrying me into a new year — perhaps metaphorically similar to the way the Greek ferryman Charon carries newly departed souls across the river from living to the afterlife — it reminded me that there is only so much I can do in my brief time on this Earth, and that there can be joy (despite the anxiety) in deciding what I find truly important. 10/10 would read again. Thank you Anna Whitney for the recommendation.

What have you enjoyed this past year? What’s on your reading list? Comment below or message me on Facebook.

Thanks for reading my newsletter! Subscribe for free updates and to support my writing.

item.title: Nicolas Cage and the Nature of Happiness
item.description: Perhaps the truest form of happiness is kindness
item.content:encoded:
This post contains mild spoilers for the movie Pig (2021).

Growing up, I watched Nicolas Cage evolve from cinema artist to legendary meme status. I still remember studying American civics in elementary school when National Treasure came out, and my fifth grade class went bananas at the discovery that we could “steal” our own copies of the Declaration of Independence from the local gift shop. “What do you want to do today?”, asked our chaperone. “Let’s steal the Declaration of Independence!”

With this backdrop of unbearable and massive talent, our cinematic legend surprised me by rendering a more serious role in his 2021 movie, Pig.

In the movie, Nicolas Cage is introduced as a solitary wilderness dweller. He hides in the woods with his only companion, an exceptionally trained truffle pig. A bucolic montage of their woodland foraging illustrates their close bond. The plot is kicked off when she is violently abducted by thieves, setting Nicolas Cage up for a Liam Neeson-esque mission to save his kidnapped friend.

The part of the film I was most intrigued by, going into the cinema, was the central relationship: Nic Cage’s connection with his pig. He is willing to risk everything — his anonymity, his safety, and even his life — to save her. In the context of a broader critique of our highly commercialized foodie and fine dining scenes, his struggle is an exploration of the powerful bonds that are possible between humans and animals. 

The final scenes of the movie complicate this theme. In them, Nicolas Cage softens the heart of an adversary by cooking a meal that reminds them of a loved one. The key ingredient of this warmhearted moment, however, is the body of a young animal hunted from the wild. As someone who has dedicated my life to the protection of animals, it frustrated me to see a movie illustrating a powerful connection between a human and an animal, yet treat a bird as a mere ingredient as though they had no story of their own.

Thanks for reading The Urban Animal! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

This made me reflect on how the writers of the movie could write such a scene with a straight face — without an overriding sense of irony that asks, why would we treat one animal’s life with meaning and discount that of another?

While the movie left this question without an answer, I did come away with two lessons. First, that food can fill our lives with kindness and meaning. And second, that our desires for kindness and meaning can underlie even our most violent behaviors.

Finding Beauty in Brutality

Towards the end, Nic Cage cooks a meal so masterfully prepared that the person he cooks it for breaks down and reveals key information regarding the plot of the movie. Through familiar scents and flavors, the food transforms a stoic culinary critic from a hostile adversary to a lonely man who is reminded of a beloved partner. On its own terms, the scene is a compelling illustration of the deep importance of connection in the human experience.

To the animal activist, however, the scene is grotesque. The meal Cage prepares is of a squab — a term for the body of a young pigeon with the developmental characteristics of an infant. In Hollywood fashion, the scene of a chef cutting into the flesh of a small bird is washed with classical music, and, in seeming contrast to the commercialized world of Portland’s fine dining scene, portrays this as a simpler, more “pure” form of experience. 

Ironically, I was watching it in the first place with friends from my animal rights circles. I was disgusted by the portrayal, and my friend exclaimed “This is bullshit!” during the scene and walked out. I wanted to do the same and felt validated that someone else had the sense to do so.

The scene was so out of place to me that it left me wondering for months: how could someone produce an entire movie about a guy fighting to save his pig, then with a straight face write a scene where the same guy cuts in to the body of an animal not so different from his own?

This pointed me toward a simple but powerful truth: that we often find deep meaning in food. 

It’s the comfort of a warm noodle soup. It is the innocent joy of a freshly steamed bao. It is the sizzling dishes we pass around to loved ones with white rice and crispy lumpia. It is the sensory binding that ties us to the people and places that fill our lives with memories and meaning. 

And that’s why this movie and this particular scene to the animal rights advocate can be so painful. Squinting from the right angle, there is beauty here. But that beauty is overwhelmed by the inescapable presence of violence.

The Meaning of Happiness

To find out whether there can be meaning amid violence, it helps to ask: when does happiness have meaning in the first place? One answer might be found in one of history’s most influential philosophers, John Stuart Mill. 

A bedrock of Western liberalism, Mill promoted a controversial moral theory that the root of all that is meaningful is simply happiness. Anything that produces more happiness, or pleasure, than its opposite, pain, is good. 

However, says Mill, not all pleasure is created equal. There is something different between binge-watching Netflix and composing a Beethoven concerto. By requiring us to overcome our instincts of what feels good in the moment, some activities strengthen our character and cultivate our abilities for more meaningful pursuits. In short, these activities result in a better form of happiness because they make us better people.

This doesn’t strike me as obviously true. Who cares if I’m playing video games rather than practicing piano, if that’s really what I’d rather do? What I do find helpful, though, is asking what kinds of things don’t simply make us “feel” the most pleasure, but leave us with a deeper sense of contentment and meaning. 

There are trends that lead us to answers. Surveys show that people often find their most meaning in life in friends and family. Research shows that a sense of connection is crucial to health and wellbeing. And one of the key drivers of motivation is the will to do good for others.

This isn’t to say that all life is about being-for-others. Happiness, as the writer Arthur C. Brooks puts it, is a healthy balance of personal enjoyment and broader goals. One of the key parts of this balance though, says Brooks, is purpose — a sense that our lives have meaning beyond our individual selves. 

The meaning of life may not lie simply in finding happiness. What we do know, however — as shown by research on happiness and the reaction of our food critic in the movie, Pig — is that the kinds of happiness that often mean the most to us are those that invoke kindness and connection with others.

The Hidden Kindness of Joy

In animal rights circles, positive experiences from food are often described as pleasure. Framed this way, the pleasure of food — done at the expense of others — can be self-evident as “selfishness”.

What our discussion of higher and lower pleasures reveals to me is how what we value as a source of pleasure may come with hidden intuitions of connection and meaning. 

The final dining scene in Nicolas Cage’s movie captures this. To the critic, his meal was not something that he simply enjoyed eating. It was tied to his memories of family and loved ones. These are memories that not only fill our lives with meaning, but may even seem to have a purpose beyond ourselves. 

The activities we identify as meaningful often relate in some way to the happiness of others. A concerto performance can exhilarate a concert hall. A memoir can share stories that cultivate our empathy. And food can, perhaps subtly, remind us of the meals we’ve shared with the ones we love. Research even shows that pleasant activities are more pleasurable when experienced with others. 

Connection with others is often our deepest, most meaningful source of joy. Sometimes what we describe as pleasure may more accurately be described as a sense of meaning. And one of the most meaningful examples of this in my life comes from my familial bond with my dog, Nikki. 

As I write this, a photo of her sits next to me at my desk. She has been my best friend growing up, so close to me that my mom calls her my sister. In her photo, she sits improbably stable as she holds her favorite toy, a basketball over half her size. She needs no words to tell me what she feels: I am happy. I am joy.

When I think of her, I am filled with a profound sense of joy and kindness. There is a distinct quality to this happiness — one I might not feel from video games or learning guitar. It is not simply pleasurable. It is meaningful. It feels as though that this is not just a higher form of happiness for myself, but somehow intertwined with deeper meanings of why we are here.

Perhaps the utilitarian philosophers, in their quest to find secular meaning, found another source of spiritual direction. The Jesuit priest Teilhard de Chardin, writing in the 1920s, said, “Joy is the infallible sign of the presence of God.” It’s the kind of happiness that makes you think, this is why we are here. We are here to love, and to be loved by others. And in these moments of shared joy, thoughts melt away and the universe suddenly seems to make sense. 

True Happiness is Kindness

The final dining scene of Pig is weird. The whole movie celebrates a guy fighting tooth-and-nail to rescue his animal companion, then ends with a depiction of violence towards animals by the same guy who through the whole movie seemed most inclined to protect them. 

There are a few lessons on happiness that I gather from this weirdness. 

First, that there are kinds of happiness that might be left out by simple understanding of pleasure. There are many ways pleasure can take shape, from joy and meaning to satisfaction and mastery and love and connection. Identifying which ones we find the most meaningful can help us live more intentional, more gratifying lives.

Second, that things that tend to be higher pleasures often connect us with others. The difference between happiness for ourselves and for others, therefore, may not be so distinct. From enjoying a meal to caring for our loved ones, the things that leave us with the deepest happiness are often those that strengthen social bonds and allow us to live kind, cooperative lives. 

Third, that even harmful behavior may come from kind, subtle values. When something feels good, we may feel it as something pure, virtuous, and moral. This intuition may be invisible to us (as are the subtle reasons for many of our beliefs). The result is that even harmful behavior might come from a hidden sense of connection with those we love.

I don’t mean in any way to excuse the violence we commit against animals for food. I have seen first-hand the atrocities of animal farming and do not believe violence against animals is justified by any amount of happiness it creates for human beings. And to me, focusing so much on the pleasure humans received from food while neglecting to show the violence behind it is a major shortcoming of the film.

What I do mean to say, however, is that we often have more understandable reasons for our beliefs than the ones we give. This realization may even give us a path towards more effective advocacy. Research suggests that activists can be more effective when they appeal to other people’s intuitively held beliefs. And finding the goodness in others can help us be more patient and forgiving when talking to people whose values differ from our own.

In doing so, we can fight for a world of plant-based food systems that resolve these tensions between violence and happiness. Where the meals we eat at family gatherings are both joyful and kind. Where the foods that fuel our cultures don’t rely on violence but are themselves symbols of compassion. 

What really emerges from this discussion, however, is a case for connection. It’s the source of some of the deepest pleasures and highest meaning we can experience. What Nicolas Cage teaches us is that one of the truest forms of happiness… is kindness.

Thanks for reading my Urban Animal newsletter! Subscribe for free to receive new posts.

item.title: How a Vegan Became Friends With a Hunter
item.description: My stubborn stand-off on a pier has a sweet ending — and offers lessons on resilience and persuasion
item.content:encoded:
Even though nothing was forcing me to stay, I felt trapped. The person I was talking to — a tall, burly man with a seemingly argumentative personality — had plenty of words and little space for my own. 

I could have walked away. Indeed, that may have been the smart move. I was getting late for work, and a disagreement on a street corner is hardly the ideal space for changing hearts and minds. But something in my brain, whether an ethical commitment to speaking against injustice or or simply an impulsive draw towards conflict, narrowed my vision to this moment right here. 

Thanks for reading The Urban Animal! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

I had met him only moments ago, and yet he felt the license to tell me hurtful, violent things. He said my friends didn’t belong here. He said they were pests. He said they even deserved to be killed! And so an argument with a stranger on a Friday afternoon became the most important thing in the world. 

With each interruption, it became harder to keep my cool. Yet I knew meeting fire with fire would do no good. I knew then that I had to make a choice. 

We have all felt trapped in a futile conversation. Maybe it’s with a family member on a sensitive topic, or a stranger at a political event. Some disagreement has ensnared your focus, and the other person seems too stubborn or closed-minded to listen to what you have to say. 

That was my situation that day. The outcome, however, was a surprisingly sweet ending. And key to that were a few tricks I’ve learned on how to navigate difficult conversations with more grace and joy.

I was walking by the Ferry Building when something to my left caught my eye. There, standing on a tourist-filled pier by downtown, was a smiling woman with a hawk perched on her arm. Standing tall and attentive, the creature was surrounded yet unfazed by a small crowd of bystanders. I joined the fray and asked the woman why she was there.

The purpose of her mission, it turns out, was pest control. The “pest” in question? The common rock dove — known simply to most as the pigeon. Companies paid her to stand there to keep pigeons away. 

As the woman described her anti-pigeon mission, a burly voice spoke up to my left. “Flying rats, I say!” 

The stocky man next to me was wearing a full black outfit topped with a leather jacket. He sported a long gray beard and spoke with a husky confidence that reminded me of someone in construction. He stood tall, somehow rising a few inches above me even as he leaned over, propping himself up on a wheelchair.

The moment the woman started explaining her mission, I felt a wave of dismay. I love pigeons. I spend my breaks at work pigeon-watching. I have even volunteered with pigeon first aid groups to “destring” pigeons, removing hair and debris from their feet that can choke blood flow and amputate their limbs. So it gave me feelings of offense and distress to hear someone describe these gentle beings I cared for as pests.

Gathering all the patience I could, my head angled as I asked them, “Why are the pigeons pests to you?”

The woman offered her perspective. She explained that pigeons can cause damage in urban environments. They are a non-native species. Their droppings can corrode equipment and spread disease. The man nodded frequently, clarifying his agreement. The woman seemed to have some sympathy for the birds; her eyes drooped apologetically when she said she tried, though not always successfully, to prevent the predatory hawk from catching and eating the smaller birds. The man was less sympathetic. To him, the pigeons were an invasive pest — no more, no less.

The man’s complaints continued to a broader topic. Namely, that the world is full of uninformed people who speak up without really understanding the issues, “like those terrorists at PETA!”, he scoffed. This one hit a bit close to home. I’ve spent much of my last few years working with animal rights nonprofits, and only weeks before this interaction, I helped record a podcast with PETA’s founder, Ingrid Newkirk.

For the first time in our conversation, I verbally registered my opposition.

“I am actually involved in animal rights circles,” I said.

My face and body language, it seems, had already given me away. The man smirked, “Oh, I could tell.” 

At this point, the conversation started to seem futile. It seemed clear where the man stood. My friends were his pests. And the people I associated with were not well-intentioned advocates, but straight-up terrorists. He didn’t seem at all interested in what I had to say, and the few words I was able to get in didn’t have much impact. There didn’t seem much point in staying.

I thought then of my choices. I could storm off from the conversation. I could interrupt him and correct what I saw were his factual errors. I could stay quiet and just nod along.

But I made a different decision. 

I realized that while I had a good sense of his ideas, I didn’t understand why he held them. I extended an olive branch, inviting peace with a spot of common ground. 

I told him that he seems to have a lot of respect and compassion towards animals. I offered, “it sounds like you would never want an animal to suffer unnecessarily.”

Before I could finish the sentence, he began nodding vigorously. “Absolutely,” he said.

That’s when he opened up to me about his story.

He grew up in the forested German countryside where his family practiced falconry and managed a plot of land. They did not own the land; on this point he was very clear. Instead, they agreed to stewardship with the owner. They could live there, living off the woods and training their predatory birds to hunt. But they were never to take more from the woods than they naturally restore. They were to be of the ecosystem, not to exploit it.

This did not immediately strike me as inspiring. Growing up, I loved animals, yet would recoil in horror at nature documentaries. There never seemed to be victory when a terrified seal escaped a starving mother polar bear. Balance matters, absolutely. But the circle of life seems of little consolation to the gazelle being eaten alive, or the field mouse rotting from disease. 

For this reason, many ethicists and biologists are calling on us to take wild animal suffering seriously. There are growing efforts in the fledgling field of welfare biology to protect the interests of animals. This includes by protecting habitats, curing diseases, and reducing starvation. It also includes, heart-warmingly to me, research on contraception for pigeons. Far from a world of immovable torment, an ideal world to me is one where we treat the suffering of animals not as an inevitable fact of life but rather one that we have the care and determination to contain.

What I did resonate with, however, was the reverence with which he spoke of his woodland duties. His upbringing brought him closer to animals, and where we could agree was that the natural world was not simply a resource for us to use — it was a community to protect.

These shared values softened my heart, and I asked more about his story with a renewed sense of curiosity. He described his career in the French Foreign Legion, an elite fighting unit known for special forces operations. It was through there that he met his wife from my own home country, the Philippines. 

This last fact perked me up. “I’m Filipino!”, I blurted out. Turns out, we shared a surprising connection — his wife may have known the woman who introduced my grandparents. They were from the same city in the same circle of friends. The connection wasn’t certain, but for a chance sidewalk encounter, the odds were surprising enough.

After this point, we didn’t talk much more about animals. We marveled at the smallness of the world and the improbability of our connection. The burly man enthusiastically told me about his frequent visits with his wife to my mother’s hometown. His stories endeared me, and we bonded over shared appreciation of the island nation’s tropical beauty and cantankerous politics.

Suspecting I was becoming late for work, I began to part from the conversation. I began to turn away, and he stopped me. “People like you and me, who share our values, we have to keep speaking up.”

Even though the conversation took positive turns, I was stunned. Moments earlier, he grouped me into a category of terrorists. And here he was, saying we were on the same team. He called me “brother” and told me to be well. He left me with a quote from Steve Jobs, commending my energy and urged me to stay hungry. 

Left feeling warm from the connection, I turned to my bike and we parted ways.

For much of my life, I fixated on petty disagreements. I was on the debate team in college, and I often turned casual encounters into bickering debates. My friends joked that Dean is a guy who can “win” an argument and “lose” a conversation. 

I’ve learned a lot since then. And that’s come with a few helpful tricks. 

First, if you’re in a tough conversation, get clear on your goal. Do you want them to adopt a specific political view? Or simply soften to where you’re coming from? Maybe it’s something else entirely, and you’d rather build or strengthen a relationship. There’s only so much anyone can change their mind in a single conversation, and clarifying our goals can take the pressure off and lead to more open conversations.

Second, focus on trust. Research shows that minds change most over time with repeated interactions with people they trust. Sometimes the first step towards changing a mind is winning a heart. You can start that by finding more commonality than disagreement and asking genuine questions to build trust.

Third, replace your anxiety with curiosity. The same part of the brain that makes us anxious is also responsible for excitement. If you feel strained, ask how you might turn that tension into curiosity. Why does this person think the way they do? What in their background may have shaped their beliefs? Think of the other person less as an agent of a harmful perspective and more as a curious mystery to solve. 

My conversation with my burly friend that day did not transform a hunter into a vegan. And it did not transform the struggles of my pigeon friends. But if nothing else, I’ll take that my afternoon stroll helped a stranger find that a young man on a pier wasn’t so much of a terrorist after all. 

This blog is inspired by The Sanctuary Initiative, a new organization I am co-founding with my friend Wayne Hsiung who is going to trial next month on felony charges for rescuing sick baby piglets from factory farms.

We combine storytelling and community building to change the world for people and animals. Read his blog here.

item.title: What, to The Universe, Is a Rescued Animal?
item.description: A longtermist effective altruist case for open rescue
item.content:encoded:
11 min read

This weekend, I’m attending my first EA Global conference, hosted by the Center for Effective Altruism. Broadly, the group organizes the effective altruist (EA) movement which seeks to use evidence and reason to do the most possible good in the world —  especially in cause areas that may not currently receive much funding or people power.

It feels a bit funny for me to be here. Increasingly, the movement is turning its eyes to the stars.

At their recent EAGxBerkeley conference (held in the beautiful and historically rich Oakland, CA), they gave each participant a copy of the latest book by Oxford philosopher Will MacAskill. In it, he lays the foundation for a longtermist moral philosophy where he argues that the single greatest moral priority of our species is protecting the very longterm future of humanity. This includes reducing existential risk (ex: nuclear war, rogue artificial intelligence). And it includes colonizing space, so there are lots and lots of humans in the future on planets beyond our own. (Elon Musk is a fan of this book.)

Thanks for reading The Urban Animal! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

With that galactic perspective, I chuckle a bit that I am here. The reason? Essentially, I work full time to rescue baby animals from abuse. I am the co-founder of a recently founded animal rights nonprofit called The Simple Heart Initiative. Recently, one of our open rescues received national media coverage, including two pieces in The New York Times, after my co-founder and his co-defendant were acquitted on felony charges for rescuing two dying piglets named Lily and Lizzie from the nation’s largest pig factory farm.

The goal is to leverage the stories of rescued animals to shift social and legal norms ultimately towards constitutional rights for nonhuman animals. It’s deeply meaningful work to me. But you may ask, if you subscribe to longtermist thinking: what does rescuing baby animals mean, in the grand scheme of the universe?

I often feel I differ from how many EA’s think. I worry too much thinking in the movement relies too much on abstract thought experiments and neglects the political implications of its ideas. But I do identify strongly with its moral case of using evidence and reason to make people’s lives better. And I found much of MacAskill’s book valuable and persuasive. There are many versions of long-termist thought, but its core idea is simple: the potential arc of the universe is long, and we should seriously reflect on our role within it. (I also have a big soft-spot for the EA movement. They were one of the first non-animal rights groups I found that takes animal suffering seriously. It’s where I’ve met many wonderful fellow vegans; and the conference food is all vegan, too!) 

This blog is an adaptation of my application to the conference describing (in roughly EA terms) how I am trying to make the world a better place. I’ll discuss:

  • Why open rescue — the act of removing animals from places of abuse and defending the practice to the public — is an effective way to do good;

  • Some of Will MacAskill’s ideas on longtermism and animals, including how to weigh the morality of nonhuman suffering and the importance of value lock-in;

  • How wild animals can benefit from open rescues of farmed animals.

Overall, it’s an edited brain dump making the case that even in the grand scheme of the universe, one of the kindest, most impactful things we can do is to rescue a baby piglet from the floor of a factory farm.

In October, two animal activists walked free after facing a decade in prison on felony charges for investigating the nation's largest pig factory farm. The #SmithfieldTrial verdict in rural conservative county in southern Utah shocked many, leading major outlets, including The New York Times, The Intercept, Democracy Now!, and others to publish highly sympathetic pieces on the trial and animal welfare.

I do this work because I believe it is effective. I believe this for two reasons. First, that animal suffering is one of the most important, tractable, and neglected (ITN) cause areas. And second, that open rescue -- as a strategy to end not just factory farming but animal suffering as a whole -- is powerful and underutilized.

Animal suffering is a key moral issue in the effective altruist ITN framework. Let’s first look at scale. The investigation in Utah, at a facility that raises over 1.2 million pigs a year, revealed that around 15% of its animals were dying before reaching slaughter. A common cause: the industry-termed "hypothermia-crushing-starvation complex". 

Essentially, mother pigs are genetically manipulated to give birth to more piglets than they have nipples. What happens to the runts who cannot compete for the limited amount of nipples? They starve. Their bodyweight falls to a fraction of their siblings, causing hypothermia that leads them to more desperately seek warmth underneath their mother. And since the mother’s metal gestation crate she will spend the rest of her life in is too small to allow her to stand up or turn around, she crushes her child.

This is an example of the suffering factory farming routinely inflicts upon trillions of animals every year. This suffering includes mutilation, crushing, overcrowding, starvation, and psychological deprivation. If Will MacAskill is correct in suggesting that neuron count is a decent approximation of welfare capabilities (which some EAs and myself believe actually undersells the issue), then in his words, the fact that "the vast majority of farmed animals... live lives full of intense suffering" may mean that the suffering of farmed animals "could well outweigh total human wellbeing."

Despite this, only a tiny fraction of our species' efforts go toward ending factory farming. In 2021, three percent of US charitable giving went to environmental and animal charities, with factory farming receiving a small proportion of those funds. And rates of vegetarianism have remained stable in the single digits for decades.

However, there is reason to believe in the historical contingency of these trends. One study by Pax Fauna suggests that one of the biggest reasons people tell themselves that factory farming will never end is a sense of futility. The rise of new technologies such as plant-based and cultivated meats can combat the sense of futility that prevents people from adopting pro-animal attitudes. 

The most exciting development to me in animal welfare, however, is the movement of open rescue. Here, I define open rescue as a strategy for social change featuring removing suffering animals from places of abuse and defending these actions in courts and to the public. Ideally, this is done in a strategic manner to shift societal values around animals. 

Only a handful of people in US history have engaged directly in open rescue. And there has been very little institutional support. With little exception, major animal welfare organizations have avoided touching open rescue with a ten foot pole, partly out of fear of controversy and legal liability. 

This thin track record means there is relatively little direct evidence for its effectiveness. Consequently, there is significant uncertainty in its ability to end factory farming. However, this also means there is significant potential opportunity. Direct evidence and broader historical trends give us reason to believe the upper range of its potential impact is very high, with evidence supporting the idea that expected value is closer to the higher end than the lower end.

For direct evidence, open rescue has led to significant positive legislation and media attention for animals. The Smithfield trial was covered widely by both national and local outlets, with major journalists demonstrating interest in covering future open rescue trials. Additionally, early journalism about the Smithfield trial from 2017 inspired an SF supervisor to pass a city-wide fur ban, paving the way for California in 2019 to become the first state and largest economy in the world to ban the sale and production of fur. More recent coverage on open rescue has also been exceptional. In response to our upcoming open rescue trial against Foster Farms, columnist Farhad Majoo at The New York Times writes:

I’m not a vegan or even a vegetarian, but as I’ve written before, vegans and animal rights activists deserve society’s immense respect rather than mockery because they are clearly right about the big issues: that industrial-scale animal farming is an incomprehensible cruelty many of us try our best not to think about, lest it ruin our lunch; that the animals we grow to eat are biologically no less complex and deserving of dignity and humane treatment than the animals we keep as pets; and that the production of cheap and plentiful meat has been an environmental and public health catastrophe whose obvious solution — eat less meat! — nevertheless remains culturally and politically verboten.

In these rescues, activists are again putting themselves on the line to establish a worthy principle.

Beyond recent media and political developments, open rescue seems effective to me because it is similar to other nonviolent direct action tactics that have historically been key to social change. The Fugitive Slave Act of 1850 may have seemed like an initial setback for the anti-slavery movement. But it triggered a backlash against slavery that turbocharged the abolitionist movement (including the Underground Railroad). That energy soon led the momentum to codify racially egalitarian values in the 13th Amendment. This dynamic of state repression sparking a progressive backlash has been seen in other movements, especially later in the civil rights movement. When advocates have the discipline and strategic capacity to leverage their own suffering for a cause, they can create  moral asymmetry that raises issue salience to the public and elites and allows them to sympathize with victims over abusers. 

The practice of open rescue forces the state (and factory farm supporters) into a decision dilemma. Do we prosecute people rescuing animals, or let them walk free? In either case, a powerful story is generated for the public. If these stories instill pro-animal sentiments in elites and the general public, they could reduce the scale and longevity of factory farming by decades or more.

To drive the point home on the urgency of shifting social norms around animals: a recent EA Forum post by Alene Anello at Legal Impact for Chickens warns that the USDA is funding research into factory farming on the moon. If they’re successful, and industrial animal agriculture is allowed to continue into the very long-term future, the implications could literally be astronomical.

The motivation for my work, however, is much broader than factory farming. It also includes the suffering of wild animals. 

Ther neuron count of nonhuman animals, driven almost entirely by fish, outweighs human neurons by a factor of seventeen. Their lives, full of predation and starvation, are likely full of incredible suffering. Will MacAskill’s briefly noted quasi-solution to this in What We Owe the Future is that hey, at least humanity is driving them to extinction. If we consider that wild animals live lives that contain more suffering than pleasure, he writes, then “we arrive at the dizzying conclusion that from the perspective of the wild animals themselves, the enormous growth and expansion of Homo sapiens has been a good thing.”

This strikes me as selling the issue, and our species, short. Research is only now scratching soil on our abilities to intervene in wild animal suffering, from pigeon contraception to pathogen mitigation. The folks at the Wild Animal Initiative allow us to envision a world where nonviolent population management limits some of the worst impulses of mother nature. 

To me, the broader vision of open rescue is that if we can shift social norms in a pro-animal direction (ex: an animal bill of rights), we can mobilize our species’ resources and ingenuity to research scalable ways to intervene in wild animal suffering. And if the technological optimism of MacAskill and Musk includes visions of a future among the stars, then I will allow my own visions to include a future of meaningful interventions in wild animal suffering.

This social norm change for animals becomes more urgent, however, when we recognize that the values of our species could well be locked in the other way. As my co-founder writes in his recent post on artificial intelligence and factory farming: “[b]efore we continue developing powerful technologies, it’s crucial that our deepest values are actually, well, good.”

There are many uncertainties for me regarding open rescue as an effective cause area. How vulnerable is the movement of open rescue to state repression or cultural backlash? How tractable is wild animal suffering? How does the intensity of factory farming weigh against the moral implications of AGI and human extinction? 

Part of this uncertainty for me is resolved by the humbling recognition that I simply care deeply about animals. I am grateful and encouraging of the work people do for other important cause areas. 

Another part is resolved by the spillover effect. If we’re lucky, social norm change for animals will increase consideration for sentience more broadly. The basic principle of animal welfare to me is that all sentience counts. If that sentience lives within an AGI, then we had better give that machine learning algorithm the respect they deserve.

Overall, whether on Earth or in the stars, animals will exist in the long-term future. Their suffering is real, in factory farms and beyond. And it should be a moral priority of our species to end it. If longtermists are correct that our future is one of fantastic artificial intelligence and GDP growth extending to the cosmos, then we can imagine that the ensuing capabilities may enable us to make a meaningful difference in wild animal suffering. This presents us with an opportunity to help our cousins of Kingdom Animalia live lives with a bit less fear and a little less suffering. And, dare I say it, perhaps even make their lives ones of happiness and flourishing.

Thanks for reading! I write to engage intellectually with people I care about. Do comment below, and subscribe to my blog to stay connected. For more writing on open rescue, check out my co-founder’s blog, The Simple Heart.
