item.title: Today I was released from jail for rescuing the Ridglan dogs
item.description: I was released from Dane County jail today where I was held for two nights for my participation in Sunday’s mass rescue at Ridglan Farms in Wisconsin.
item.content:encoded:
I was released from Dane County jail today where I was held for two nights for my participation in Sunday’s mass rescue at Ridglan Farms in Wisconsin. I am still wearing the clothes I was arrested in, which were returned to me still damp from the rain. I wrote this post while in jail.

It is freezing in the rain, with bits of hail coming down on me. I am surrounded by police, accompanied by over twenty activists at Ridglan Farms, a notorious dog testing and breeding facility. The police tell us if we leave the facility, they won’t arrest us. We are not sure what to do.

Two days ago, I joined nearly a hundred activists in walking into the second largest dog breeding and research facility in the United States. We walked onto the property in broad daylight to rescue the animals inside. Ridglan Farms has been a site of public controversy for years for confining thousands of beagles for cruel experiments, including force feeding them commercial laundry detergent and surgically ripping out their eye glands without anesthesia. The abuses are so bad that a local court ordered them to be prosecuted for felony animal abuse.

Subscribe to my free newsletter, The Urban Animal, to receive new posts and support my work.

Under immense public pressure, the district attorney cut a deal with Ridglan: avoid prosecution if you relinquish your license to sell dogs for research. Ridglan said yes. But the deal still allowed the company to conduct research on animals and did nothing to protect the roughly two thousand dogs still trapped at the facility who could be euthanized or simply sold off for further experimentation.

In response, hundreds of people, including nearly every animal rescue and humane society in Wisconsin, signed an open letter to District Attorney Ismael Ozanne asking him to protect the dogs currently trapped at Ridglan.

The district attorney refused to act. So we did.

Around 8:30am on Sunday morning, our convoy of six passenger vans pulled up to Ridglan Farms. About a hundred of us entered the facility, using angle grinders and crowbars to cut through fencing and enter buildings that held beagles for research. There were too many of us for Ridglan employees to stop, and even as police arrived, we were able to remove twenty-two beagles who were successfully loaded into vans and taken to safety.

Under normal conditions, I would be deeply uncomfortable with our actions. I tend to be a rule-follower by nature. I was a Boy Scout growing up and played guitar for years in my church choir. In the weeks leading up to the rescue, I feared how it would look for us to use sledgehammers and crowbars to break into a building, even if it was necessary to help those inside. But as I sit now after my second night in jail, I know that what we did was not just morally right, but legally right.

Pursuant to state and federal law, it is permissible to take otherwise unlawful actions under the “necessity doctrine” to prevent a greater evil or significant bodily harm to someone else. The question now before the courts, in the case of myself and dozens of other activists who took nonviolent action to protect dogs who were victims of felony abuse, is whether animals are “someone,” or merely “something.”

SHARE: Viral videos on Instagram and TikTok of the Ridglan beagle rescue

That question is at the heart of why we are here. For far too long, our legal system has treated animals as mere things to use and abuse. They are confined by the millions across the country in tiny metal cages too small to stand up or turn around. They are packed into trucks and cargo ships huddling in their own feces to be torn apart at slaughterhouses. And in the case of the Ridglan dogs, they are injected with rabies and forced to live their entire lives in a two-by-four foot wire cage.

That has to stop. That is why we are here: to directly rescue animals from harm, even if that means going to jail. If we can nonviolently draw attention to corporate animal abuse, we can challenge the treatment of animals as property under the law and drive a broader conversation about whether animals are simple objects or rather sentient creatures worthy of dignity and respect.

This is a difficult fight. But for the thousands of Ridglan dogs, and the countless other animals trapped in cages around the world, it is a fight worth having.

Before my arrest, I was about to give up. After the initial dogs were rescued, over twenty of us walked back onto the property to gather more dogs. We were stopped by police as we attempted to re-enter one of the breeding buildings and were detained for over an hour. They told us if we didn’t leave, we would be arrested. I felt our group’s morale waning as we stood there, shivering under ice and rain, deciding what to do.

Then we heard the cries of dogs crying and wailing through an open window only feet away from where we stood. We decided then that we weren’t leaving — not without the dogs. I told my fellow activists, as well as the officers who detained us, “We wouldn’t want someone to give up on us. So we’re not going to give up on them.”

The officers looked away in seeming acknowledgement of their defeat. Shortly after, a dozen more police officers arrived and moved towards us with zip ties. They tied our hands behind our backs, put us into squad cars, and booked over twenty of us into Dane County jail where Wayne, Alexandra, Aditya, Raquel, and myself remain locked up on criminal charges awaiting a court hearing and possible felony trial.

We are eager to be a voice for animals in a court of law where their voices have been too long denied. I am confident that even if we continue to be trapped in a cage, that our actions will inspire a broader conversation that will help every animal be freed from theirs.

The Ridglan dogs are worth it.

I have been released from jail and am anticipating possible filing of criminal charges against myself and my fellow arrestees. The story of the mass rescue of beagles from Ridglan Farms has only begun. For more, follow me on Instagram as well as Wayne Hsiung, my co-arrestee and lead organizer of the Ridglan beagle rescue, on Substack and social media (Instagram and Facebook.

What’s Next (updated)

  • We are RETURNING to Ridglan with 1000+ people to save every remaining pup at Ridglan Farms in a final mass open rescue on April 19. Sign up here to learn more!

  • I’ll be speaking next Thursday evening at Mox, a social impact co-working space in San Francisco, with attorney and fellow Ridglan arrestee Abie Brauner. Come through and bring your friends!

Thanks for reading The Urban Animal! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

item.title: I sent my mugshot to my boss. He loved it.
item.description: You’re less likely to lose your job for rescuing beagles from Ridglan Farms than you think
item.content:encoded:
I was moments away from telling my new boss that I might be in jail next week on felony charges.

I had no idea what he would say.

I had just joined the election campaign of Alan Wong, a San Francisco city supervisor. I didn’t know anyone on the team before applying. And this wasn’t an activist campaign. Alan is a moderate in a city with closely guarded reputations and politics so cut-throat that they’re described as “a knife fight in a phone booth.”

So I thought associating my activism with the candidate would be a non-starter.

Maybe I shouldn’t tell my boss, I thought. I’m 28 years old with nothing but a social science degree and a future career to protect. Better he just never found out?

Then I thought of advice from Wayne, an animal rights attorney and fellow activist, who said the biggest risk to my career would be appearing dishonest. Telling them upfront, he said, was the key.

So I took a risk and told my boss.

The Urban Animal is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free subscriber.

“I do a lot of progressive activism in my personal time,” I said, “and I don’t want it to conflict with the campaign.”

“Tell me more,” he said, his hands in his pockets and eyes on the ground as we walked.

So I did.

I told him everything. That I’d be joining an activist group next week at Ridglan Farms, a lab that confines thousands of beagles their entire lives in 2 x 4 foot wire cages and for surgical experiments without anesthesia. That the District Attorney refused to protect the victims, even after a judge found probable cause of felony animal cruelty at the facility. And that I was planning to break in next week with about a hundred activists to rescue the dogs myself — and would likely be arrested on felony charges.

He took it all in and said… that’s awesome!

He even suggested I invite Supervisor Alan Wong to be part of the rescue.

I was shocked at his support. I asked whether government staffer roles are more sensitive than campaigns. He said ones with more conservative supervisors might be. “Nowhere you’d want to work anyway,” he said, and added that being arrested for nonviolent activism in this city was a “badge of honor.”

A couple weeks later, I was sitting in a living room with Supervisor Alan Wong and his government staff cheering over videos of me on the news getting out of jail.

The risk is lower than you think

Would-be activists have often told me they can’t risk arrest because they’re worried about losing their job.

My general sense is people believe the risks are higher than they are.

Before last month’s rescue at Ridglan Farms, about 180 people had been arrested at mass open rescues in U.S. history. Fewer than 10% were ever charged. Only two activists were convicted — both after choosing to go to trial and rejecting all plea deals by the prosecution.

I was a senior in college when I was first arrested on felony charges with over fifty activists for rescuing chickens from a poultry farm in 2018. The prosecutor offered to drop my charges. I threw the offer letter in the trash, eager to stand trial for rescuing animals from criminal abuse. I never heard from the District Attorney’s office again.

I know only one person who lost their job for an arrest at a mass open rescue. He was a school teacher and had his job re-instated shortly after.

Professional licenses

Maybe you’re a lawyer worried about losing your license. (I only know of lawyer examples here.)

Wayne Hsiung is the only professional I know whose license was affected by nonviolent rescue activism. He has faced decades worth of felony charges, stood trial three times, and is now a two-time convicted felon for rescuing animals.

He is still a licensed attorney in the State of California, pending results of his felony convictions.

His law license was temporarily suspended after being convicted of felony burglary for sneaking into a farm in North Carolina to take a sick baby goat to the vet. His license was later re-instated, pending resolution on his appeals for both both felony convictions. He has since lost his goat case appeal. The State Bar of California is waiting for the results of his second appeal for a mass chicken rescue before making a next decision on his license.

My young lawyer friend Taj had a similar but less intense experience. After applying to become a lawyer in Arizona, he was called in for a character review after being arrested for rescuing a starving baby goat from a Whole Foods factory farm.

He said he couldn’t promise he wouldn’t do it again. They admitted him anyway.

Travel restrictions

These are among the most real consequences I know of.

Wayne Hsiung, for example, has been denied entry to Canada after his convictions and has not been admitted since.

For myself, I’ve been arrested twice on felony charges — burglary, conspiracy, and grand theft from open rescues at chicken and duck factory farms in 2018 and 2019. Since then, I’ve traveled internationally to seven countries without issue, including my home country of the Philippines and a successful visa application in Vietnam.

In my experience, travel restrictions for nonviolent animal activism come after convictions, not arrests.

Financial consequences

There can also be financial risk.

In some cases, courts have ordered significant criminal restitution after convictions — sometimes exceeding $100,000.

For example, activists like Wayne Hsiung and Zoey Rosenberg have faced six-figure restitution orders tied to open rescue cases.

That said, it can be complex and difficult for animal-abusing companies to actually force you to pay restitution, even after a conviction. Neither Wayne nor Zoey have paid a dime in restitution.

From open rescue activists I talk to, this is one of the most serious concerns, and it’s worth taking seriously. That said, restitution only comes after a conviction. If you are arrested, you are unlikely to be charged unless you are clearly in high-level leadership, and will still have opportunities to plea out.

Some jobs might be stricter. Just ask.

At least one person I know works with a mayor’s office in another state and was told they could participate in the next Ridglan Farms beagle rescue — but only in roles that would not risk arrest.

My friend Taj also said his big law job offer was deferred after he told them upfront. They were supportive of his advocacy for an “important cause,” but decided his charges would need to be resolved before he could start.

So for some jobs, there is more risk.

The good news is you don’t have to guess.

My advice is to just be upfront that you’re considering standing up for your values, and see what they say.

What about the reward?

When I was standing in the rain last month at Ridglan Farms, I considered walking away. I was detained with over a dozen activists for more than an hour, freezing in the rain, with the police saying they would arrest us if we didn’t leave.

Then I heard their cries. Dogs were wailing through an open window only feet from where I stood. They were trapped in cages, never having felt anything soft in their lives.

I knew I couldn’t leave.

I knew I would regret it if I did.

So I stayed. I told the police and my fellow activists, “We wouldn’t want someone to give up on us. So we’re not going to give up on them.”

I spent the next two nights in jail.

And it was one of the most powerful experiences of my life.

—

From what I can tell, it could also be one of the most potentially transformative moments in the history of animal rights.

The rescue has garnered tens of millions of views on social media. We’ve gotten remarkably positive press coverage from CNN, USA Today, and Washington Post. Wayne Hsiung, who was arrested for organizing the last Ridglan rescue, has drawn support from Ricky Gervais and Jen Welch, one of the nation’s most important political podcasters.

Personally, I was interviewed by Wisconsin news coming out of jail and later by Muni Takes, an up-and-coming San Francisco media channel that has featured several local politicians.

I’ve been an animal rights activist for nearly a decade now. I know how difficult it is to shine light on corporate laboratories and factory farms which confine and mutilate billions of animals across the country. And the Ridglan beagle rescue has created a rare and powerful opportunity for change.

—

I will say — even if I had lost my job, this all would have been worth it.

I stepped back from the Alan Wong campaign after last month’s rescue to volunteer full-time for the upcoming rescue this Sunday, April 19. Over two thousand people have signed up to return to Ridglan Farms and get each of the thousands of dogs stuck there out of cages.

I told my boss I’d be stepping back, with my career uncertain and unsure of how I’d financially support myself afterwards.

He said, “I’ll always give you a job.”

This is a historic moment for animals. Don’t miss it.

Your boss — and the Ridglan pups — might love you for it.

item.title: I am in jail again for trying to save the Ridglan dogs
item.description: Saturday’s tear-gassing of peaceful rescuers at Ridglan Farms shows how far authorities will go to protect corporate abuse.
item.content:encoded:
This was posted by Dean’s friends while he was in Dane County jail. It was transcribed over the phone.

My left eye still stings from tear gas and pepper spray by riot police. My hand is numb from the hours it was tied behind my back in a squad car.

Today is my third straight day held on felony burglary charges in Dane County jail. I was here only a few weeks ago after myself and 100+ activists nonviolently rescued nearly two dozen beagles from Ridglan Farms. Ridglan is the second largest breeding and research facility in the nation, and it has subjected thousands of dogs to criminal animal abuse, including injecting them with rabies and removing eye glands without anesthesia.

Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work

Even though 27 of us were arrested last time, we returned with roughly 1,000 people determined to save them all.

And I thought we would.

There was overwhelming public support after the last rescue. Millions of people expressed support on social media and thousands signed up to join us at the next rescue. Even Ridglan’s Congressperson Mark Pocan refused the company’s calls to stop activists and urged the safe rehoming of the Ridglan dogs. It seemed clear that the public was on our side.

So I was shocked this week when a thousand of us volunteer rescuers were met on a Saturday morning by riot police and tear gas.

I arrived in a van at the farm shortly after other activists with a press-badged reporter by my side. Almost immediately, a sheriff’s officer approached me in a gas mask and pepper sprayed me directly in the left eye. I clenched my eye, nursed my wounds, and carried on.

For the next few hours, I marched with waves of peaceful grandmothers repeatedly back into clouds of tear gas determined to get past the barbed wire fence and riot police to save the dogs.

How can police be so violent to peaceful advocates?

Well, Dane County Sheriff Kalvin Barrett gave us the answer. I watched him on the news from my jail cell as he claimed that we violently aimed to harm police officers, and that his duty was to protect business and property. In this case the business interests are very powerful. The biomedical industry transacts millions of dollars in Dane County every year, in large part through research at the University of Wisconsin-Madison.

And this industry seems intent on coming down on us hard.

After last month’s rescue, the National Association for Biomedical Research, a powerful industry lobbying group, called for us to be prosecuted as terrorists under the Animal Enterprise Terrorism Act (AETA).

That may be why, for my first time in years as an activist, I was pulled in for questioning by state level investigators. On Saturday, I was brought into an interrogation room by two special agents wearing all black uniforms from the Wisconsin Department of Justice. My fellow activist, Wayne Hsiung, is being held separately from me in the same jail, and was similarly visited this weekend for interrogation by the FBI.

A part of me is scared. I am 29 years old and facing felony burglary charges. I do not know how much more of my life I might spend in a cage. But then I feel compelled to act when I think of the millions of animals in laboratories across the country who spend their entire lives in a cage.

I am optimistic that we will soon bring these abuses to an end. People around the world are outraged by what they see happening to the Ridglan dogs. Grandmothers are walking into tear gas to save the most vulnerable creatures on Earth. And politicians are increasingly treating animal rights with the seriousness that it deserves.

This morning, I joyfully sobbed, even though my tears stung from pepper spray still in my left eye, when my lawyer told me by phone that a leading candidate for Wisconsin governor had just called for the safe release of all the dogs at Ridglan Farms.

I know waves of change are coming soon. I do not know that they will come soon enough to keep me out of a cage.

What I do know is that right now there is a mother in a cage at Ridglan Farms. She has never gone outside or looked up at the sun. The district attorney who has sworn an oath to protect her has turned his back on her, allowing her and her children to be sold off for experiments or simply killed to spite the people who care about her. She is one of the thousands of pups still at Ridglan Farms right now. And she needs your help.

So I am asking you to please contact the Wisconsin Attorney General and ask him to protect the thousands of victims of ongoing felony abuse at Ridglan Farms.

If we can save those dogs, then no matter what happens to me, this all will have been worth it.

UPDATE FROM DEAN: I am out of jail! The court ruled that I am “dangerous” and released me on conditions including $10,000 in bail and a no-contact order with my four co-defendants, Wayne Hsiung, Aditya Aswani, Misha Lunsky, and Melanie Brieno. We are eager to argue for the right to rescue in court.

Follow me here and on Instagram, and stay tuned through Wayne’s Substack and savethedogs.io for the Ridglan mass beagle rescue trial. Onward! Let’s save the dogs!
